explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Ethan says, “in the heavens You establish Your faithfulness.” Think about that. He's not pointing at a building or a hill. He's pointing straight up, as high as you can look.

Good guess, because a temple sounds like a natural spot for something that important. But Ethan never mentions a temple in this verse. He says, “in the heavens You establish Your faithfulness.” Even a really tall roof can't beat that.

I get why you'd pick a mountain, friend. Mountains feel like holy ground. But Ethan doesn't name any mountain here. He says, “in the heavens You establish Your faithfulness.” and the heavens are a lot higher than any peak.

explanations.answer: His offspring and throne would endure
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. God swore, “I will establish your offspring forever and build up your throne for all generations.” Look at who gets the promise: David, Israel's king, and the family line that follows him. That's a long-lasting oath, one that reaches well past David himself.

explanations.answer: He would build a temple for the LORD
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd pick it, friend, because building something sounds like a big royal job. But this oath never mentions a temple. What God swears here is about David's offspring and throne. “I will establish your offspring forever and build up your throne for all generations.”

explanations.answer: He would never have to face death
explanations.explanation: That one would be a whale of a promise, but it's not in the verse. The oath is about what comes after David: his offspring and his throne, lasting for all generations. God says, “I will establish your offspring forever…” So the promise reaches past David himself and out to the people who come after him.

Close, but Ethan says the opposite. He asks, “For who in the skies can compare with the LORD? Who among the heavenly beings is like the LORD?” I think he's asking those questions because he knows the answer is nobody. No heavenly being gets to stand up and say, "I'm basically the same."

Yep, friend. Ethan asks, “For who in the skies can compare with the LORD? Who among the heavenly beings is like the LORD?” He doesn't name a single contender. I think the answer he has in mind is that nobody in the skies comes close.
There it is, baker. Ethan says, “O mighty LORD, Your faithfulness surrounds You.” Notice that this word has been popping up since verse 1. Ethan can't stop talking about it, and I can't blame him.

Thunder sounds right for a mighty LORD, I'll give you that. But Ethan never says thunder in this psalm. He says, “…Your faithfulness surrounds You.” It's a quieter word, and it's the one he keeps coming back to.
Wisdom is a fine word, friend, but it isn't the one here. Ethan says, “O mighty LORD, Your faithfulness surrounds You.” Faithfulness is the star of this psalm, and Ethan mentions it again and again.
That's it, baker. Ethan says, “You rule the raging sea; when its waves mount up, You still them.” The waves are piling up, and the LORD stills them. That's what ruling the raging sea looks like.
Nope, friend. The verse puts the LORD in charge of the sea: “You rule the raging sea…” When the waves mount up, He doesn't stand back and watch them crash. Ethan says, “…You still them.”
I can see how raging waves might push you that direction. But Ethan says the LORD rules the raging sea. “when its waves mount up, You still them.” So the waves go quiet instead of getting taller.
Not quite, baker. Ethan says, “The heavens are Yours, and also the earth.” He doesn't hand the earth off to anybody. He adds, “The earth and its fullness You founded.”
Correct, friend. Ethan says, “The heavens are Yours, and also the earth.” Nothing in the verse leaves any part of it to somebody else. He keeps going: “The earth and its fullness You founded.”
You got it, baker. Ethan says, “Tabor and Hermon shout for joy at Your name.” These are two whole mountains, and they're shouting! Ethan says they do it at the LORD's name.
Trembling would make sense with big mountains, friend, but that's not what Ethan says here. He says, “Tabor and Hermon shout for joy at Your name.” It's a cheer, not a shake.
I get the picture, but the mountains aren't bowing in this verse. Ethan says, “Tabor and Hermon shout for joy at Your name.” They're loud and happy about it.
Yes, baker. Ethan says, “Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne…” A foundation holds everything else up. So these two are what the whole throne rests on.
A big throne does sound like it'd come with riches, friend. But Ethan never says that. He says, “Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne…” The word you're looking for is justice.

Armies would be an easy guess for a throne, I'll admit. But that isn't the word in this verse. Ethan says, “Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne…” So justice is the one that fits the blank.
Right, baker. Ethan says of those blessed people, “They rejoice in Your name all day long…” All day long! That's a lot longer than my attention span during a timer countdown.
Not this time, friend. Ethan says of those blessed people, “They rejoice in Your name all day long…” So it's true, and it's the whole day, not just one part of it.
That's right, baker. Ethan says, “Surely our shield belongs to the LORD, and our king to the Holy One of Israel.” The king belongs to the Holy One. That's who he answers to.
I see why you'd go that way, friend, but Ethan doesn't say the people hold the king. He says, “…our king to the Holy One of Israel.” The king belongs to Him.

An army guarding a king makes sense, but it's not what the verse says. Ethan says, “Surely our shield belongs to the LORD, and our king to the Holy One of Israel.” The king belongs to the Holy One, not to the soldiers.
That's it, baker. God says, “I have bestowed help on a warrior; I have exalted one chosen from the people.” So the one He helped is a warrior. And He says that warrior was chosen from the people.
Priest is a fair guess, friend, since God is picking someone special. But the word God uses is warrior. He says, “I have bestowed help on a warrior…” The vision doesn't call him a priest.
I can see why you'd think of a prophet, since God is speaking in a vision. But He doesn't use that word for this man. He says, “I have bestowed help on a warrior…” The one He helped is a warrior.
Yes, baker. God says, “I have found My servant David; with My sacred oil I have anointed him.” David, Israel's king, was set apart with oil. That's what anointing is.
Healed would fit oil in some places, friend, but this verse doesn't say it. God says, “with My sacred oil I have anointed him.” The oil is for setting David apart, not for healing.
Cleansed sounds like a thing oil might do, I'll give you that. But God's word here is anointed. He says, “with My sacred oil I have anointed him.”

Not quite, baker. God says the opposite: “No enemy will exact tribute; no wicked man will oppress him.” So no enemy gets to make David pay up. That's a promise, and it goes with God's other promises about strengthening him.
Correct, friend. God says, “No enemy will exact tribute; no wicked man will oppress him.” So no enemy collects tribute from David, and no wicked man oppresses him. That's what the LORD promises him.

explanations.answer: Over the sea and the rivers
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. God says, “I will set his hand over the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers.” Earlier Ethan said that the LORD rules the raging sea. Here God puts David's hand over it.

explanations.answer: Over the hills and the valleys
explanations.explanation: Hills and valleys sound like a good spread of land, friend. But that's not what God says here. He says, “I will set his hand over the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers.” It's water, both the sea and the rivers.

explanations.answer: Over the cities and the fields
explanations.explanation: That would be a lot of territory, but those aren't the words in the verse. God says, “I will set his hand over the sea, and his right hand upon the rivers.” So it's the sea and the rivers.
Yes, baker. God says, “He will call to Me, ‘You are my Father, my God, the Rock of my salvation.’” David calls out to God as his Father. That's a close, warm way to talk to Him.
Not this time, friend. God says, “He will call to Me, ‘You are my Father, my God, the Rock of my salvation.’” So David does call Him Father. That's right in the verse.

explanations.answer: Deal with it using the rod
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. God says, “I will attend to their transgression with the rod, and to their iniquity with stripes.” So He doesn't ignore it. He says He'll take care of it Himself.
I can see wanting that to be true, friend. But God says, “I will attend to their transgression with the rod, and to their iniquity with stripes.” He doesn't promise to look the other way.

That's a heavy guess, but it isn't what God says. He says, “I will attend to their transgression with the rod, and to their iniquity with stripes.” Earlier He promised, “I will establish his line forever…” So the rod isn't the end of the line.

Not quite, baker. God says, “But I will not withdraw My loving devotion from him, nor ever betray My faithfulness.” Even with the rod in verse 32, He keeps His loving devotion. He doesn't take it away.

Right, friend. God says, “But I will not withdraw My loving devotion from him, nor ever betray My faithfulness.” He does deal with the sin, but He doesn't pull His loving devotion from David. Both things are in the same promise.
Yes, baker. God says, “Once and for all I have sworn by My holiness…” Then He says, “…I will not lie to David…” He swears by His own holiness, and that's about as solid as an oath gets.
Kingdom sounds like a big thing to swear by, friend, but it's not in the verse. God says, “Once and for all I have sworn by My holiness…” So the word that fits is holiness.
I get why you'd think so, but God doesn't swear by the people here. He says, “Once and for all I have sworn by My holiness…” He swears by His own holiness.

That's right, baker. God says David's offspring shall endure forever, and his throne is “…like the moon, established forever, a faithful witness in the sky.” So the moon follows the sun in the promise. Sun and moon, both lining up with that throne.

Stars would fit the sky nicely, friend, and I know a thing or two about stars. But they aren't named in this verse. God says the throne is “…like the moon, established forever, a faithful witness in the sky.”
Dawn is a pretty guess, but it's not the word here. God says the throne is “…like the moon, established forever, a faithful witness in the sky.” The second light He names is the moon.

That's what Ethan says, baker, and I think this part hurts. He tells the LORD, “You have renounced the covenant with Your servant and sullied his crown in the dust.” After all those promises, it's a hard thing to say out loud. Ethan says it plainly anyway.

I wish it read differently, friend, but Ethan does say it. He tells the LORD, “You have renounced the covenant with Your servant and sullied his crown in the dust.” That's a hard verse. I think Ethan is saying what he sees, even though it's heavy.
Right, baker. Ethan says, “You have exalted the right hand of his foes; You have made all his enemies rejoice.” So the king's enemies are the ones on top here. It's a hard verse to read.
Sons did come up earlier in the psalm, so I see why you'd pick them. But that's not who Ethan names here. He says, “You have exalted the right hand of his foes…” The foes are the ones lifted high.

I can see why you'd think of the people, friend, but the verse points somewhere else. Ethan says, “You have exalted the right hand of his foes; You have made all his enemies rejoice.” It's the foes whose hand is lifted.
Yes, baker. Ethan says, “You have bent the edge of his sword and have not sustained him in battle.” A bent sword doesn't help much in a fight. It's a hard picture.
A shield did show up earlier in the psalm, so I see the pull. But in this verse, it's the sword. Ethan says, “You have bent the edge of his sword and have not sustained him in battle.”
A scepter sounds right for a king, friend. But Ethan doesn't say it here. He says, “You have bent the edge of his sword and have not sustained him in battle.”
Yes, baker, and it's a heavy line. Ethan says, “You have ended his splendor and cast his throne to the ground.” He's naming it straight. The throne God once promised to build up is on the ground.
I wish it were false, friend. But Ethan says, “You have ended his splendor and cast his throne to the ground.” That's a heavy thing to read. Ethan says it out loud to the LORD anyway.

explanations.answer: How long will You hide Yourself
explanations.explanation: That's what he asks, baker. Ethan says, “How long, O LORD? Will You hide Yourself forever? Will Your wrath keep burning like fire?” After all that rubble, he asks the LORD directly. I think that's an honest thing to do.

explanations.answer: Why did You choose David at all
explanations.explanation: I can see that question coming out of such a sad moment, friend. But Ethan doesn't ask it. He asks, “How long, O LORD? Will You hide Yourself forever?” He's asking how long, not why.

explanations.answer: Who will sit on the throne next
explanations.explanation: That's a practical question, but Ethan doesn't ask it. He asks, “How long, O LORD? Will You hide Yourself forever? Will Your wrath keep burning like fire?” His question is aimed at the LORD Himself.

Close, baker, but Ethan isn't saying that. He asks, “What man can live and never see death? Can he deliver his soul from the power of Sheol?” Sheol is the place of the dead. I think he asks it because the answer is nobody.

Right, friend. Ethan asks, “What man can live and never see death? Can he deliver his soul from the power of Sheol?” Sheol is the place of the dead. I think the answer he has in mind is nobody, and it fits with his plea that his life is brief.

explanations.answer: The loving devotion He swore to David
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Ethan asks, “Where, O Lord, is Your loving devotion of old, which You faithfully swore to David?” It's the same loving devotion he started singing about in verse 1. Now he asks where it is.

explanations.answer: The crown He placed on David's head
explanations.explanation: The crown is in the psalm, so I see why you'd go there. Back in verse 39, Ethan says it was sullied in the dust. But in this verse he asks about “…Your loving devotion of old, which You faithfully swore to David?”

explanations.answer: The mighty army that served David
explanations.explanation: An army would be a big thing to miss, friend, but Ethan doesn't ask about one. He asks, “Where, O Lord, is Your loving devotion of old, which You faithfully swore to David?” That's what he wants to know about.

Yes, baker. Ethan closes with, “Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and amen.” Remember how he began by singing of the LORD's loving devotion forever? He ends on forever too. That's a lot of heartache with a lot of praise on the other side.

explanations.answer: He asks for a new king
explanations.explanation: Asking for a new king would be a natural next step, friend, but Ethan doesn't do that. He ends the psalm with, “Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and amen.” The last word goes to blessing the LORD.

After all those hard verses, I see why you'd think so. But Ethan ends the psalm differently. He says, “Blessed be the LORD forever! Amen and amen.” He opened the psalm with singing forever, and he closes with blessing the LORD forever.
